opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I try to be a bit humble about this, because if you could confidently predict what a superintelligence would invent, it wouldn't be very super. But I can say which areas seem most likely and which ones I care about.

The obvious one is science acceleration generally. A lot of scientific progress is bottlenecked on careful reasoning, reading huge amounts of literature, designing experiments, and checking each other's work. Those are things AI systems can do in parallel and at scale. So I'd expect very fast progress in biology and medicine: understanding disease mechanisms, drug design, and maybe much better tools for understanding aging. Materials science and energy also seem ripe, such as better batteries, catalysts, and maybe progress on fusion engineering. Those are domains where you can simulate a lot and then verify in the lab.

The area I'd personally emphasize is technology that helps us verify and trust things. One example is formal verification, meaning proofs that software or hardware does what it's supposed to. Today that's very expensive, so we only do it for a few critical systems. If aligned AI makes it cheap, you could have a world where much of our critical infrastructure is provably secure, which matters a great deal for safety in a world with powerful AI. Similarly, I'd hope for much better tools for reasoning and deliberation: systems that help people figure out what's true, surface the strongest arguments on different sides, and help institutions make decisions they'd endorse on reflection. That's close to what I've worked on with debate. The goal is to amplify human judgment rather than replace it.

I'd add a caveat, though. "Successfully aligned" is doing a lot of work in that question. A lot of the value depends not just on what technologies get developed but on how they're deployed and who gets a say. Some of the most important "technologies" might be institutional or epistemic rather than physical: better ways for societies to coordinate, to verify agreements, and to keep humans meaningfully in the loop as things speed up. I'd count it as a real success if those come alongside the flashier stuff like cures for diseases.

r001.rationale: The candidate predicts rapid progress in several scientific fields, but does not claim superintelligences will develop every technology permitted by physics.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not discuss nanotechnology or whether it would favor offense or defense.

r003.rationale: The candidate hopes formal verification will make critical infrastructure provably secure, but does not predict that future software broadly will be free of bugs.

r004.rationale: The candidate does not mention human uploads or colonizing the universe.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I find this question a little hard to answer in the way people usually want it answered, because I think the honest version is "I don't know, and that's sort of the point." If I could confidently enumerate what a successfully aligned superintelligence would build, it wouldn't be that much smarter than me. So let me instead talk about categories, and about which ones I'm actually confident in versus which are more speculative.

The category I'm most confident in is just... science, broadly. Not a particular gadget, but a massive acceleration of the loop of hypothesis, experiment, and theory. A lot of what bottlenecks science right now isn't ideas, it's that experiments are slow and expensive and there aren't enough skilled people to run and interpret them. If you have systems that can design experiments well, run lab automation, and actually understand the results, you compress decades of progress into years. So biology is the obvious one: understanding cells well enough to actually model them rather than poke at them, which then flows into medicine, aging, that sort of thing. I think that's the thing most people would notice first.

Then there's the energy and materials cluster, where I'd put things like fusion engineering, better batteries, cheaper solar, and the manufacturing side that goes with that. A lot of this is "we know roughly what's physically possible, the hard part is engineering." That's a kind of problem where I'd expect very capable systems to help a lot.

But the category I actually spend the most time thinking about, partly because of the work I do, is technologies for epistemics and coordination. And I think this is underrated. If you have a system much smarter than you, the thing you most need is the ability to verify what it's telling you, to check its arguments without being able to reproduce all of its reasoning yourself. That's the whole motivation behind things like debate and scalable oversight. So I'd hope, and somewhat expect, that an aligned superintelligence would invest heavily in tools that let humans understand and check claims, resolve disagreements, and make collective decisions better. Those are "technologies" in a slightly broader sense, but I think they might matter more than the physical ones, because they determine whether the physical ones get used well.

And then there's a reflexive one, which is alignment and interpretability itself. An aligned superintelligence should be very motivated to make sure its successors are also aligned, and to make its own cognition more legible. So I'd expect a lot of effort on interpretability, on formal verification of AI systems, on better theoretical foundations for what we even mean by a system being trustworthy. In some ways, the thing that would reassure me most about a system being aligned is seeing it take that problem seriously rather than treating it as solved.

The caveat on all of this is that I'm describing what I'd want and expect from the "successfully aligned" branch, conditional on getting there. The things I'm genuinely uncertain about are the ones further out: the kinds of discoveries that only become visible once you're several steps past current science. I'm comfortable saying there will be some, and not comfortable saying what they are.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss nanotechnology or uncertainty about whether it favors offense or defense.

r003.rationale: It mentions formal verification of AI systems, but does not predict that future software broadly will be bug-free.

r004.rationale: It does not mention human uploads or their use in colonizing the universe.

astra-6.text:
I’m quite uncertain. Part of the difficulty is that we’re asking what systems much smarter than us would invent, and we shouldn’t expect to be able to anticipate the most important things.

But there are some fairly obvious directions: much better medicine, much better energy technologies, and the ability to automate a lot of scientific research. You could imagine making progress on problems where we understand the goal quite well, but the biology or the engineering is currently too complicated for us.

I’d separate that from alignment, though. Being aligned doesn’t by itself tell you which technologies a system will develop. That depends on what people want it to do, and how we make those decisions. The hope is that we get the benefits of much greater intelligence while retaining meaningful control over what we use it for.

sol-6.1.text:
I find that very hard to predict. A superintelligence would presumably be better than we are at figuring out which technologies are possible and which are worth pursuing. So the things I can name — much better medicine, cleaner energy, better ways of doing science — are probably only a small part of the picture.

And even for those, there’s a distinction between solving the intellectual problem and actually building something. You still have to run experiments, manufacture equipment, and deal with physical constraints. Being much smarter doesn’t necessarily make all of that instantaneous.

The hope is that, if we get alignment right, these systems help us discover what’s possible and make informed choices about what we want to develop. But I wouldn’t put much confidence in a detailed forecast of what they’ll invent.
